NBC News: Death in Haditha (6 January 2007)

JURIST: Iraqi lawyer related to Haditha victims blasts $2,500 US 'compensation' payments (4 June 2006)

content.p: On 19 November 2005, a roadside bomb struck a United States Marine convoy in Haditha, a town in western Iraq.One Marine was killed. Within minutes, Marines shot dead Iraqi civilians in the street and in two houses. The killings later became known as the Haditha massacre, and NBC News later described the criminal prosecution as the biggest U.S. case involving Iraqi deaths to come out of the war.

Haditha had been a hard place for the Marines long before November 2005. NPR's timeline of the case says a roadside bomb there killed 14 Marines in August 2005, and that the town was a Sunni stronghold with intense insurgent activity. The Marines in the convoy that morning were on a routine run to bring fresh Iraqi troops to a checkpoint.

The bomb went off as a white sedan was waved to the side of the road. The blast killed Lance Corporal Miguel Terrazas, 20, of El Paso, who was driving the fourth Humvee, and left another Marine trapped in the wreckage. NBC News, citing a Naval Criminal Investigative Service report that ran to thousands of pages, reported that the Marines who rushed to help said they took rifle fire from several directions.

The narrative NBC News drew from that report, which the Washington Post had obtained, described five men taken from a white taxi. According to U.S. and Iraqi witnesses quoted in it, Wuterich shot them one by one after the Marines ordered them out, and another Marine fired into their bodies as they lay on the ground. Wuterich told investigators that he shot the men because he considered them a threat. A Marine who was there said the men had been standing in a line when they began to fall.

The Marines then went into two houses. The Marines told investigators that they believed they were authorised to fire freely after insurgents fired on them. Sworn statements said an officer had ordered them to take one of the homes, and that Wuterich had told them to shoot first and ask questions later. Marine officials, as NBC News reported, said the troops had not identified their targets before throwing grenades and firing into the two houses, where 14 unarmed people died in roughly ten minutes. A 13-year-old girl said she played dead and survived the attack on the second house. Her account, as reported, was that she lost five other members of her family in the room.

The first public account was different. NPR reported that the Marines' preliminary report, released on 20 November 2005, blamed an improvised explosive device for killing 15 Iraqis and one Marine. The civilian count was later revised to 24, including 11 women and children.
content.h2: A story that took months to surface
content.p: The Marines did not open a criminal inquiry for several months. NPR's timeline says an Army colonel, Gregory Watt, was appointed on 14 February 2006 to lead a preliminary inquiry, and that his report of 3 March recommended further investigation. On 12 March, Lieutenant General Richard Zilmer, the top Marine commander in western Iraq, decided the evidence was enough for a full criminal investigation and asked the Naval Criminal Investigative Service to carry it out.

Time magazine had begun asking military sources about the incident in February 2006. NPR's timeline describes Time's March 2006 report as the first to piece the whole story together, from the Iraqi allegations of a massacre to questions about how the incident was reported up the Marine chain of command. NBC News's later account said that senior officers in Iraq, one of them a major general, learned of the civilian deaths almost at once but did not begin a probe for months.

Political reaction followed quickly. On 17 May 2006, U.S. Rep. John Murtha, a former Marine, said in a news conference that the troops had "killed innocent civilians in cold blood." On 28 May, he disclosed on television that the Marines had made condolence payments to the families, at a time when the official explanation was still a roadside bomb. NPR reports that he called Haditha "worse than Abu Ghraib." Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki said on 30 May that the killings were not justified and expressed remorse. The next day, President George W. Bush said, "If in fact, laws were broken, there will be punishment."
content.h2: Charges against the squad and the officers
content.p: In December 2006, four Marines were charged with murder. NBC News reported that Wuterich faced 13 counts of unpremeditated murder. Three others were also charged with murder: Dela Cruz, a sergeant, and Sharratt and Tatum, both lance corporals. Their lawyers argued that the men had behaved properly in a confused fight, and that the civilian deaths were a tragic but unavoidable part of fighting in a dangerous area. Dela Cruz's attorney declined to comment.

Four officers were charged with failing to investigate and fully report the killings. The highest-ranking of them, Lieutenant Colonel Jeffrey Chessani, was the officer the case turned on. NBC News reported that no officer of higher rank had faced a combat-related court-martial since Vietnam.

The officers' cases fell apart on a question of process. On 17 June 2008, Colonel Steven Folsom, the military judge, dismissed the charges against Chessani after finding that a four-star general overseeing the case had been improperly influenced by an investigator. NBC News reported that the investigator, Colonel John Ewers, later became a senior legal adviser to General James Mattis and attended legal meetings where the charging decisions were discussed. Mattis testified about the matter two weeks earlier. Folsom said: "Unlawful command influence is the mortal enemy of military justice." The charges were dismissed without prejudice, which meant they could be refiled, and Folsom barred Marine Forces Central Command from any further role in the case.

By that June, only one of the eight Marines originally charged was still facing prosecution. KPBS and NBC News both reported that Wuterich was the last defendant, and NBC called it the largest American criminal case over Iraqi deaths arising from the conflict.

The case came to court six years after the killings. On 23 January 2012, Wuterich pleaded guilty to one count of dereliction of duty. NPR's Pentagon correspondent, Tom Bowman, said the offence was fairly low-level. He said the plea carried forfeiture of pay and a reduction in rank, and that Wuterich could face up to three months in jail.

Bowman said the case had simply fallen apart over time. In his account, the prosecution lacked forensic evidence and witnesses. The military had offered immunity to some of the people involved in exchange for testimony, but some of those witnesses ended up favouring the defence, describing a hostile environment and saying they could use deadly force. He added that some prosecutors were faulted for not pressing the case harder, and that six years had passed. Some Marines he spoke to were upset, he said, because they believed 24 innocent people had been killed and no one faced stiff punishment.

At the sentencing hearing, Wuterich apologised for the loss of the families' loved ones and said he had never meant to harm them. In an unsworn statement, he said: "But even with the best intentions, sometimes combat actions can cause tragic results." He also said his guilty plea did not mean his squad had behaved badly or dishonourably.

WNCW reported that the military judge planned to recommend the maximum sentence allowed, 90 days of confinement. Lieutenant Colonel David Jones told Wuterich: "It's difficult for the court to fathom negligent dereliction of duty worse than the facts in this case." Under the agreement, as WNCW reported, a demotion was possible, but Wuterich would not spend any time in jail. A Marine Corps spokesman said the officer who decided to accept the plea bargain, and to stipulate that Wuterich receive no jail time, would give no public explanation for it.

The families' experience of the payments is documented mainly through a lawyer who spoke for them. In June 2006, the lawyer Khaled Salem Rsayef, who was related to several of the victims, denounced by videotape the $2,500 that the U.S. military had paid each family for each person killed. He called the sum insufficient. JURIST reported that such sympathy payments were made by local commanders without any admission of liability and were capped at $2,500 per person.

Rsayef also said that, at the first meeting between the families and U.S. officers in November 2005, the officers told relatives that the victims had died from an insurgent's roadside bomb, not from gunfire by American troops. That account is Rsayef's own, and it is given here as his claim.

The Iraqi cabinet decided in early June 2006 to open its own inquiry, and Maliki said he would ask Washington for its files. The reporting available here does not say what the Iraqi inquiry concluded, or whether the families received more money later.

The number of people killed was reported differently at different stages. The preliminary Marine report counted 15 Iraqi dead, while the later count was 24. The NBC News narrative of the investigators' findings describes five men at the taxi and 14 people in the houses, and those two groups do not on their own add up to 24. Charge descriptions also differ: NBC News reported unpremeditated murder in 2007 and voluntary manslaughter in 2008, while NPR wrote that the murder charge was reduced to manslaughter. Those are the accounts of the outlets named, and they should be read with their dates in mind.

Some accounts treat the Marines' conduct as a massacre. Others, including Wuterich's defence, held that the houses were hostile, that the Marines were under fire from several directions, and that the deaths were tragic but not criminal. No court found any of the Marines guilty of murder. The only guilty plea in the reporting cited is Wuterich's, to one count of dereliction of duty.
